blurb: Grown entirely for its foliage: a low aromatic subshrub of feathery silver-grey leaves that stays evergreen through the winter. CSU calls the bloom insignificant, and it is — this is a texture and colour plant, and a very tough one.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
seasons: Aromatic feathery silver foliage year-round, evergreen through winter; bloom insignificant
wildlife: Grown for foliage; bloom is insignificant and of little pollinator value

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 10,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil, and lean. It is a plant of dry plains and rocky slopes; rich or wet ground makes it lax and short-lived.[1]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–24 in wide. Aromatic feathery silver foliage on an evergreen subshrub, with what CSU calls an insignificant bloom.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers negligibly — it is grown for foliage; CSU records the colour as insignificant (it is a foliage plant) and the height as 8–24 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Because the flowers are negligible, treat this as a foliage plant: shear it lightly in spring to keep the mound tight, and never cut back into bare old wood, which will not resprout reliably on a woody-based *Artemisia*.[1]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: Aromatic and long used ceremonially and medicinally, but not a food — Artemisia species carry thujone and related compounds.[1]
edible.caution: This guide does not treat fringed sage as food. The genus has a long ceremonial and medicinal record across the Plains and Southwest, but *Artemisia* species characteristically contain thujone and related volatile compounds, which are neurotoxic in quantity — the same chemistry that makes its Eurasian relative absinth wormwood (*A. absinthium*, a Colorado List B noxious weed) something to handle carefully. Enjoy the scent on your fingers; don't brew it, and don't give it to children or anyone pregnant or nursing.[1]
